analysis.one_liner: Funds housing and services for homeless people and taxes luxury property sales, secret buyers, and giant landlords.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or hearing; it sat in five House committees and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023, with 21 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would channel roughly $27 billion a year into programs for homeless and housing-cost-burdened households, including new construction of deeply affordable housing, public bathrooms, and legal help. It would bar federal homelessness money from cities that criminally punish people for sleeping outside, and it would pay for the programs with three new taxes: 5% on sales of $10 million-plus property, 10% on property bought through anonymous shell entities, and 1% of rent collected by landlords owning thousands of units. It also funds voting access and document replacement for homeless people and makes the federal homelessness council permanent. The bill never got a hearing or vote in any of the five committees it was referred to.
analysis.who_benefits: Homeless and housing-unstable people, and households paying too much of their income in rent, would get new grants for housing construction, shelters, services, and alternatives to policing. Cities would get money only if they stop arresting people for sleeping in public and safeguard homeless people's belongings. Homeless people would also get help voting and replacing lost IDs and documents.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a Community Development Block Grant Plus program to fund construction of housing affordable to people earning 30% or less of area median income, plus public bathrooms, water fountains, and places to rest [S3].

Authorizes about $27 billion a year across homelessness programs: up to $10 billion each for Emergency Solutions Grants and Continuum of Care grants, $6 billion for CDBG Plus, $1 billion for emergency food and shelter, $100 million for alternatives to criminalizing homelessness, and smaller library and voting-access grants, partly backfilled by the new property taxes [S3].

Bars federal homelessness funds from any government that enforces criminal punishment on homeless people for sleeping outside or on public property, and requires procedures protecting homeless people's property under the 14th Amendment [S2].

Imposes a 5% tax on sales or exchanges of real property worth at least $10 million, a 10% tax on property transfers involving anonymous entities whose owners are not in public records, and a 1% tax on rent collected by landlords owning more than 1,000 units in one metro area, 2,000 units total, or 500 units across three states, with the tax waived in jurisdictions that have rent control, just-cause eviction, or source-of-income protection laws [S2].
Funds grants to help homeless and housing-unstable people vote and a study of barriers to voting and to replacing essential documents like IDs [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Sellers and buyers in high-end real estate ($10 million-plus deals split a 5% tax), buyers using anonymous shell entities (10%), and large corporate landlords (1% of rent). Revenue from these taxes is credited to HUD homelessness programs, with general appropriations covering the rest of the authorized spending.
analysis.who_pays_short: Luxury sellers, shell-company buyers, big landlords

drawbacks.text: The three new taxes add transaction costs to high-value real estate and could raise costs for some buyers and sellers; the mass-landlord rent tax could be passed through to tenants in areas without rent control or just-cause eviction laws, since the tax does not apply where those tenant protections exist [S3].

The authorized spending (about $27 billion a year) exceeds the revenue credited from the new taxes, so general appropriations would have to cover the balance, adding to federal deficits unless new money was appropriated [S3].
Conditioning federal funds on ending enforcement of camping bans could tie cities' hands on managing public spaces while grant money is phased in, a tradeoff local officials would have to weigh [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefits are large and targeted at the poorest households: housing construction, shelter capacity, and an end to punishing people for sleeping outside. The main costs fall on wealthy property sellers, opaque buyers, and large landlords, though some of the rent tax could reach tenants in unprotected markets, and taxpayers generally would fund the gap between authorizations and the new revenue. On balance it is a substantial transfer of resources toward homeless and rent-burdened people, paid for disproportionately at the top of the property market.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to five House committees the day it was introduced, got only a single subcommittee referral in late 2022, and expired when the Congress ended without any committee vote or floor action.

narrative.text: Rep. Pramila Jayapal introduced the bill on June 8, 2021, joined by 16 other House Democrats as original cosponsors [S1].
The bill was referred the same day to the Financial Services, House Administration, Judiciary, Education and Labor, and Ways and Means Committees [S5].
It gathered 21 cosponsors in total, all Democrats [S4].

The only further action in the bill's life was a November 1, 2022 referral to the Judiciary Subcommittee on the Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties; no committee reported the bill and the House never voted on it before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large corporate landlords, luxury property sellers, and buyers using anonymous shell entities avoided the new taxes, and no new federal money flowed to homelessness programs.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large landlords and luxury property sellers

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; none of them chaired a committee that moved it to a vote

sides.party_line_note: All 21 cosponsors were House Democrats and no Republican signed on; the bill never reached a floor vote, so no roll call exists to measure the split.

industries.note: A 1% tax on all rent collected by owners of thousands of units, though waived where rent control, just-cause eviction, or source-of-income laws exist. The tax never took effect because the bill died.
A 5% tax on transfers of $10 million-plus property, split between buyer and seller, with the proceeds credited to HUD homelessness programs. The bill's death left these transactions untaxed.
A 10% tax on property transfers to or from entities whose beneficial owners are not in freely accessible public records, aimed at secret ownership of real estate. The bill died before it could apply.

industries.industry: Nonprofit homeless and housing service providers
industries.note: Would have been eligible for grant funding for diversion programs, crisis teams, shelters, and services, subject to new training and non-discrimination conditions.
